newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - German motor market price war.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - German motor market price war.

text.p: In the last nine days the two leading insurers in the German motor market, Allianz and HUK-Coburg, both published their 1996 figures. Against the odds, Allianz managed to achieve a net gain of 40,000 to 8.0 million insured vehicles. HUK-Coburg, on the other hand, lifted its portfolio by 280,000 from 5.83 million to 6.11 million.

While it means Allianz is no longer losing business, the company cannot be happy about the present situation. Its growth is fragile, and it really has not managed to turn the tide. Low-cost operators led by HUK-Coburg are still on the attack, and they are gaining market share.

HUK-Coburg chief executive Rolf-Peter Hoenen believes that his company's prices undercut Allianz by about 10 to 11 percent - despite the latter's heavy rebates and numerous incentive-driven sales campaigns. HUK-Coburg has clearly accepted the challenge and has matched Allianz' price cuts - a fact reflected in the motor premium volume, which went down by 1.6 percent from 4.29 billion marks to 4.22 billion marks, although the number of insured risks went up.

Despite all this, both HUK-Coburg and Allianz achieved underwriting profits for 1996. But Hoenen had to admit that this was unlikely to be the case in 1997. The 1996 price cuts were offset by the exceptional loss situation, which was very favourable for insurers. But loss figures are unlikely to go down further at the same speed as prices.
The true battle is now beginning, and it looks quite possible that no firm will make money in motor insurance for some time.
Allianz is set to offer a low-cost tariff, which is priced 10 percent below its already-discounted standard rates, thus aiming precisely at the clientele of the low-cost providers.

Once underwriting losses are produced, the question arises who can hold out longest. In favour of the low-cost operators is their cost structure, mainly the absence of an expensive, commission-driven structure of tied agents. But most of them lack the possibility to compensate for motor losses with profits from other sectors.

Motor accounts for 87 percent of HUK-Coburg's non-life business, for Allianz' domestic non-life operation, the figure is 42 percent. And: HUK-Coburg as a fast- growing company has not quite the reserve strength that Allianz can muster. The German motor market is in for exciting times.
